moon_01_first_explorers.t: For thousands of years, humanity looked towards the Moon, wondering what existed beyond the darkness.
In 1959, the Soviet spacecraft Luna 2 became the first human-made object to reach the lunar surface.
Seven years later, Luna 9 achieved the first successful soft landing, sending photographs back to Earth.
America's Surveyor spacecraft followed, studying the lunar soil and preparing the way for human exploration.
They were small machines carrying an enormous responsibility.
They had no passengers, no return journey, and no promise of survival.
Their mission was simple, reach another world and tell humanity what was waiting there.

moon_02_apollo.t: The next chapter changed human history.
NASA's Apollo program sent astronauts towards the Moon aboard the powerful Saturn V rocket.
The command and service modules carried them through space.
The lunar module brought them down to the surface.
In 1969, Apollo 11 made the first crewed lunar landing.
But these machines were never designed to bring every part of themselves home.
The descent stages remained on the Moon.
The ascent stages carried astronauts back towards orbit before eventually being discarded.
Their lunar roving vehicles carried astronauts across the lunar landscape, exploring places they could never have reached on foot.
Today, those three rovers remain parked on the Moon.
Their final passengers returned to Earth.

moon_03_lunokhod.t: While astronauts explored the Moon, another kind of explorer traveled across its surface.
The Soviet Union sent robotic machines that could move without a human on board.
In 1970, Lunokhod 1 arrived on the Moon.
Controlled by engineers on Earth, it traveled across the lunar landscape, capturing photographs and studying the soil.
It survived for months, far beyond its original planned mission.
Its final resting place remained uncertain for decades, until scientists located it in 2010.
It traveled farther, examined craters, and collected valuable scientific information.
But during its journey, lunar dust covered part of its radiator after it entered a crater.
Its temperature rose, and its mission came to an end.
Two robotic explorers, two journeys across another world, and two machines that never returned home.

moon_04_change.t: Decades passed, but the Moon was never forgotten.
China's Chang'e program brought a new generation of robotic explorers.
In 2013, Chang'e-3 delivered the Yutu rover to the lunar surface.
It began exploring, examining rocks and sending scientific information back to Earth.
In 2019, Chang'e-4 achieved the first successful soft landing on the far side of the Moon.
Its companion, Yutu-2, began exploring terrain that no rover had previously visited.
It traveled across an ancient landscape, slowly collecting information about a mysterious region hidden from direct view of Earth.
Then came Chang'e-5, which collected lunar material and returned it to our planet.
In 2024, Chang'e-6 achieved the first successful sample return from the lunar far side.
The landers and robotic systems that made these achievements possible remained behind when their missions ended.
New explorers had arrived, and more machines had become part of the Moon's silent history.

moon_05_chandrayaan.t: The exploration of the Moon was no longer limited to the world's earliest space powers.
In August 2023, India's Chandrayaan-3 mission achieved a historic lunar landing.
Its Vikram lander carried the Pragyan rover to the lunar surface near the south polar region.
Pragyan examined the surface, studied the lunar soil, and conducted scientific experiments.
When the lunar night arrived, the mission's planned surface operations ended.
Attempts to re-establish communication were unsuccessful.
Japan also introduced a different kind of lunar explorer.
The SLIM spacecraft demonstrated precision landing technology in January 2024.
It deployed two small robots, LEV-1, a hopping robot, and LEV-2, a transforming miniature explorer known as SORA-Q.
They showed that lunar exploration did not always require enormous machines.
Sometimes, even the smallest explorers could make history.
Their missions ended, but the technology and discoveries they left behind became part of humanity's continuing journey.

moon_06_silent_moon.t: Today, the Moon holds the remains of generations of exploration.
The descent stages of Apollo landers still stand at their landing sites.
The lunar roving vehicles remain where astronauts parked them.
Lunokhod, Yutu, Pragyan, and other robotic explorers have left their marks on the lunar surface.
Not all of them failed.
Some completed their missions exactly as planned.
Others stopped working before anyone expected, and some never made it safely to the surface at all.
Every machine had a purpose.
Every journey demanded years of engineering, testing, and sacrifice.
Yet the engineers who built them could never accompany them forever.
They watched from millions of kilometers away as their creations explored, discovered, and eventually fell silent.
Perhaps the saddest part is that these machines cannot come home.
They remain beneath the same sky, surrounded by the dust and silence of another world.
But they are not meaningless pieces of abandoned technology.
They are monuments to human curiosity.
They came from Earth.
They explored the Moon.
And even after their final transmissions, their stories remain.
Somewhere on that distant world, the explorers are still waiting.
Welcome to Forgotten Explorers.
